name: AI behaviour drifts from the principles
problem: An AI agent asked to do work applies the principles inconsistently, and nothing shows how often. It builds a framework for a one-off fix, treats a task as a problem, merges use cases whose best differs into one function, drops the qualifier from a rule it restates, or pastes a fifth copy, and the instructions meant to prevent this (a skill, a system prompt) are edited with no measure showing whether the behaviour got better or worse.
who_has_it: People who direct AI agents and want their principles applied (Joshua, a team lead), the authors of the skills and prompts that carry those principles, and the agents themselves, which start each session without memory of earlier corrections.
why_it_matters: AI writes most of the work, so reading every reply or implementation does not scale, and a principle that is not applied is not a principle. Structure that people can steer only by reading output brings back the problem that structure exists to remove.
why_hard: Replies are open-ended; acting by a principle often means holding back from adding structure or keeping a qualifier; the same words can be used while doing the opposite; models vary between runs and versions; and each live measurement costs money.
existing_attempts: Writing the principles into a skill or a system prompt, correcting the agent in conversation, reading samples of its output by hand, public language-model benchmarks and eval tools (promptfoo, OpenAI Evals, LangSmith). They test general ability or one prompt at a time, and do not tie a measure of adherence to which instructions are used.

name: No order to follow
problem: People who want to apply ESOI have the five record types and the principles but no order to follow. They do not know what to do first, write implementations before deciding what best means, trust a metric nobody checked, skip the perspectives that would find gaps, and stop after the first build instead of looping back.
who_has_it: Anyone applying ESOI to a project, product, course, process or code for the first time, the AI agents asked to apply it, and people who apply it often but skip steps under time pressure.
why_it_matters: The records only optimize an intent when they are made in an order that decides best before building and keeps measuring after; without an order, ESOI is applied partially and the parts that address the biggest risks are the ones skipped.
why_hard: The work is a network, not a line, so any order is a simplification; small tasks and large projects need very different depth; and the order has to change as ESOI itself changes.
existing_attempts: The 2020 Project Documentation board checklist (an order, but without metric checks, interfaces, the split test, perspectives or retirement); the one-hour guide in this repository (a short pass, no full order); general project-management and design-thinking processes, which do not compare implementations by metric.

name: Applied structure is rediscovered
problem: Where ESOI is already applied, how those projects relate and where to look in each is rediscovered in every session.
who_has_it: People and AI agents who apply ESOI to more than one project on the same machine or board.
why_it_matters: Time goes to finding structure that already exists, and a new session may build again what a neighbouring project already solved.
why_hard: Projects live in different places, use different layouts and change, so any list written once into the guidance goes stale and names projects the reader does not work on.
existing_attempts: Routing rows written into a skill's index for known projects, a project's own CLAUDE.md, and memory of past sessions.

name: Behaviour verdicts uncalibrated
problem: A model that grades whether a reply acts by the principles can disagree with the people whose intent the principles express, can favour its own phrasing when it wrote the reply, and can pass a reply that uses the right words while doing the opposite. Nothing shows by how much, so a score built on its verdicts looks like evidence but may measure the judge.
who_has_it: Joshua and others who review the behaviour metric to steer, and the maintainers who choose instructions by that metric.
why_it_matters: A miscalibrated judge makes the behaviour metric steer toward whatever the judge likes. A reviewer who finds its verdicts wrong stops trusting the metric and goes back to reading output, which is the problem of untrusted measurements again.
why_hard: The people whose verdicts would calibrate it are few and their time is the scarcest input; the labelled replies are written by the same author as the checks, so agreement can be circular; and a judge changes whenever the model behind it does.
existing_attempts: Pattern checks alone, which agree with their author by construction; using the strongest available model as judge without measuring it; agreement statistics on small samples; hand review of every verdict.
